newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's troubles far from over in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia's troubles far from over in Chechnya.

text.p: Whoever wins elections in Chechnya on Monday, the outcome will be a ringing vote for secession which reminds Russia that its troubles are far from over in the rebel region.
All 16 candidates in Chechnya's presidential race advocate independence from Russia, putting them on collision course with Moscow, which rules out secession.
Leaders of both sides say they are determined to avoid more bloodshed after a 21-month conflict and they see elections as a step towards stability in the North Caucasus region.
But an agreement to defer a decision on Chechnya's status, in or out of Russia, for five years is a potential time-bomb which could explode if the sides do not tread carefully.

"Whoever comes to power in Chechnya, in any situation, Chechnya will conduct itself as an absolutely independent state," said General Lev Rokhlin, chairman of the Russian lower house of parliament's defence committee.

"Russia will not agree to sovereignty for Chechnya and Chechnya will do all it can to confirm its sovereignty," Rohklin, one of Russia's senior officers in Chechnya before he resigned to take up politics, said in a television interview.

Moscow and separatist leaders agreed to the elections for a regional president and parliament under a peace accord signed last August after tens of thousands of people had been killed in fighting between separatists and Russian forces.

The agreement allows for a five-year breathing space in the dispute over Chechnya's status, something which critics say is deeply humiliating for Russia and which delays inevitable new clashes over independence.
Supporters say the deal may not be perfect, but something was needed to stop the bloodshed, and talks on Chechnya's status will be easier in peacetime.
Russian officials publicly deny there is any chance that Chechnya will be allowed to secede, but one minister has warned his government colleagues not to be complacent.
"I think there is a real threat that Chechnya could split from Russia," Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said this month, suggesting steps should be taken to brake such moves.
Russian officials hope the relatively moderate Aslan Maskhadov, until recently Chechnya's prime minister, will be elected president.

The Kremlin's nightmare scenario is victory for Shamil Basayev, a radical former field commander who led a hostage-taking raid in southern Russia in June 1995 in which his troops fought Russian forces and more than 120 people died.

Some political analysts say the Kremlin might refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the vote if Basayev wins and that it would justify this by citing Chechnya's failure to create conditions for refugees outside the region to take part.

"Moscow is preparing itself for the day when it might not be apt to recognise the new (Chechen) president," Valery Yakov, a commentator with the liberal newspaper Izvestia, told NTV commercial television.
Even if a moderate wins, Russian officials would have to tread carefully.

The Kremlin wants stability in Chechnya, and is ready to grant it almost complete autonomy within Russia. But it also wants to be tough enough on Chechnya to discourage other independence-minded regions from seceding.
The Chechens also have to be wary. They want independence, but they may have to soften their rhetoric because of the need for Russian money and business to rebuild Chechnya's economy.

Thorny issues include the reparations which Chechnya seeks from Moscow but which have shown little sign of reaching their destination. Tension could also be raised by any problems at talks on releasing the last prisoners of war.
Another danger is that the so-called "parties of war" on either side -- those who made money from the fighting, for example through arms trading -- might try to restart the conflict.
Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov has already said he will not let ethnic Russians be mistreated in Chechnya.
"If it comes to a real genocide in Chechnya, it is Russia that should protect Russians there and save them from arbitrary rule even by sending troops," he said last week.
